title: Constant Coefficients: Complex Roots
short: e^(αt)(c₁ cos βt + c₂ sin βt) from Euler's formula.
trouble: Students use the whole complex root in the cosine, writing cos((α + iβ)t).

blocks.html: When $b^{2} - 4ac < 0$, the characteristic equation has complex roots $r = \alpha \pm \beta i$. The exponential $e^{rt}$ still solves the equation, but it is complex-valued. Polar form and Euler's formula $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ turn it into real solutions.

If the roots are $\alpha \pm \beta i$ ($\beta > 0$), the general solution is $$y = e^{\alpha t}(c_1\cos\beta t + c_2\sin\beta t).$$ The real part $\alpha$ sets growth or decay; the imaginary part $\beta$ sets the angular frequency.

By Euler's formula, $e^{(\alpha + \beta i)t} = e^{\alpha t}e^{i\beta t}$ $= e^{\alpha t}\cos\beta t + i\,e^{\alpha t}\sin\beta t$. Call this $u + iv$. The coefficients $a, b, c$ are real, so $L[u + iv] = L[u] + iL[v]$, and this is 0 only if both $L[u] = 0$ and $L[v] = 0$. So the real and imaginary parts are real solutions, with $W = \beta e^{2\alpha t} \ne 0$. (The other root $\alpha - \beta i$ gives the same pair again.)

Writing $\cos((\alpha + \beta i)t)$ or $e^{\beta t}\cos\alpha t$. Only $\beta$, the imaginary part, goes inside the cosine and sine; the real part $\alpha$ goes in the exponential. A check: the solution must be real, and its envelope $e^{\alpha t}$ must shrink when $b > 0$ (positive damping).

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $y = e^{at}\cos bt$ with the envelope $\pm e^{at}$ dashed. The real part $a$ stretches or shrinks the envelope; the imaginary part $b$ changes how fast it oscillates. With $a = 0$ the swings never die out.

blocks.name: trigwave
blocks.cap: The solution $2\cos 3t - 2\sin 3t$ of the second example is one cosine wave: $2\sqrt{2}\cos\left(3\left(t + \frac{\pi}{12}\right)\right)$, amplitude $2\sqrt{2}$.
